title: Why the World Has Time Zones
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: When it is noon in Tashkent, it is seven in the morning in London in winter, ten in the morning in Moscow, and three in the afternoon in Beijing. These differences are caused by the rotation of the Earth, which turns once every twenty-four hours, so that the sun rises in the east before it rises in the west. For most of history, nobody needed to worry about the difference. Each town set its clocks by the sun, with noon defined as the moment when the sun was highest in the sky. The coming of the railway, however, made this system impossible, and led to the creation of the time zones that we use today.

In the early nineteenth century, a traveller going from one town to another found that the local time changed with every few kilometres: if he travelled west, noon arrived later, and if he travelled east, it arrived earlier. This was only a small difficulty for people on horseback, but for the railways it was a nightmare. A timetable that listed the departure of a train at ten o'clock had to say in whose time. In Britain, railway companies solved the problem in the 1840s by using a single time, which was London time, throughout their network, and soon most towns adopted it for everything.

The problem was even greater in North America, which is wider than Britain, and where there were hundreds of local times in use in the 1870s. Railway companies used more than fifty different times, and passengers had to change their watches again and again. In 1883, the American railways introduced four standard time zones, each one hour apart, and almost all of the country adopted them within a year. By dividing the country into broad belts, they solved the problem without going to the extreme of using a single time for the entire continent.

The world followed. In 1884, delegates from twenty-five countries met in Washington to agree on a prime meridian, a line of zero longitude from which all others would be measured. They chose the line which passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, near London, partly because most of the world's shipping already used it on charts. The Earth was divided into twenty-four zones, each fifteen degrees of longitude wide, since the sun appears to move through fifteen degrees every hour. Time in each zone is set by counting hours ahead of or behind Greenwich Mean Time, which is today replaced by Coordinated Universal Time.

In practice, zones are not straight lines on the map. Countries draw the boundaries to suit themselves, so that a region does not have two times. China, which is as wide as the continental United States, uses a single time throughout the country, and in winter the sun rises in the far west of China at about ten in the morning by official time. Russia, the largest country, has eleven zones. Some countries use zones that differ from their neighbours' by half an hour or forty-five minutes: India is five and a half hours ahead of Greenwich, and Nepal is five hours and forty-five minutes ahead.

Uzbekistan lies in a single zone, five hours ahead of Greenwich, and it does not change its clocks in summer. Many other countries put the clocks forward by an hour in spring to take advantage of longer evenings, a practice called daylight saving time, although its benefits are disputed and a number of countries have abandoned it. The zones also meet at the International Date Line, which runs roughly along the line of 180 degrees of longitude in the Pacific. A traveller who crosses it from west to east repeats a day; one who crosses it from east to west loses a day.

Dr Anton Weiss, a historian of science, says that the time zones are a good example of how technology forces people to cooperate. Before the railways and telegraph, nobody saw any reason to agree on the time; afterwards, the advantages were so great that countries accepted a single system. Today the internet and global trade are creating a need for still greater co-ordination. Computer systems around the world use Coordinated Universal Time to record events, so that a transaction in Tashkent and one in Toronto can be placed in order. Dr Weiss adds that although the time is a human invention, the Earth's rotation, which makes the day, is not.
